column1: # Rakudo, measured ONCE PER RELEASE — not once per Raku++ tag.
# Rakudo ships monthly, so between two of its releases this column is a
# CONSTANT. Measuring it per Raku++ release drew ordinary run-to-run noise as
# if it were signal: up to 19% on sortby, whose lane is bimodal (~168/198ms)
# on this machine, and 2-10% elsewhere. gen-dashboard now assigns these values
# by DATE, so every point between two Rakudo releases — tagged, untagged
# sitting, or main — carries the same number and the line is a step function.
# Measured 2026-08-31, Darwin 24.6, Apple M3, macOS 15.7.4. Each Rakudo built
# from source, native arm64, one toolchain for all three. 20 timed runs per
# kernel after a discarded warm-up, all three eras interleaved inside every
# round; FOUR such passes, and the value below is the minimum across all 80
# runs. Convergence was checked, not assumed: min(pass A,B) against an
# independent min(pass C,D) moved by at most 1.8% and by more than 2% on
# none of the 48 values. A two-pass check had disagreed by up to 10% because
# the passes ran as sequential blocks and tracked the machine's drift; the
# minimum over four interleaved passes removes it.
# NOTE MoarVM has no JIT backend on arm64 (it compiles src/jit/stub.o), so
# these are NOT comparable with a rakudo column measured on an x86_64 host.
# era      released    kernel      ms
# `mainwhen` joined the kernels on 2026-09-20, after the sitting above, so its
# reference was measured that evening instead — by a different and weaker
# method, which is why it is fenced off here rather than folded in above. It is
# the minimum of 36 runs across six separate harness invocations spanning an
# hour (the main sitting's three passes plus five release-artifact runs), not
# the 80-run four-pass interleave the rows above use. The six invocations spread
# 284.0-290.4 ms, 2.3%, which is the same order as this file's stated ~2% noise
# figure. Measured against the homebrew arm64 bottle rather than a from-source
# build; the same evening's loopsum control landed within 3.5% of the row above,
# so the two references agree well enough for one line on one chart. There is no
# `rakuast` twin: that lane was not run for this kernel.
# A FIFTH COLUMN: the compiler backend a row was timed under.
# Rows without it are `legacy` — every row above, Rakudo's historical compiler.
# Rows below carry `rakuast`: the SAME release compiled through RakuAST, the new
# frontend that Rakudo 2026.09 makes the default and that 2026.08 reaches with
# RAKUDO_RAKUAST=1. Not a second engine, the same binary with one environment
# variable set. (From 2026.09 the interesting variable becomes RAKUDO_LEGACY=1
# instead; only the lane table in the measuring tool needs to know.)
# Measured 2026-09-01 by tools/measure-rakudo-modes.raku, on THE VERY BINARY the
# legacy column above was measured with — the 2026-08-31 sitting's own
# from-source arm64 build, not a rebuild of it: 20 timed rounds x 4 passes, the
# two lanes interleaved inside every round, warm-up discarded, the value being
# the minimum across all 80 runs. Convergence checked as the header above
# prescribes — first two passes against the last two, worst 1.3%, none over 2%.
# All 16 kernels were verified to print identical output in both lanes before
# anything was timed; the tool refuses to time a kernel where they differ.
# SCALE. These rows are their own sitting, a day after the one that produced the
# legacy column, so the sitting's own legacy lane was measured alongside as the
# check: it reproduced the committed column above within -0.7% to +1.9% (mean
# +0.6%), straddling zero, which is run-to-run noise rather than a systematic
# offset. The two columns are on one scale; a ratio read off the chart is good
# to about a percentage point. The legacy column is deliberately NOT rewritten
# from this sitting — 2026.06 and 2026.07 were measured with it in one
# interleaved sitting, and replacing 2026.08 alone would put one era on a
# different day's noise from its neighbours.
# WHICH arm64 build, settled by measurement rather than by the note in
# BENCHMARKS.md. Three arm64 v2026.08 builds timed against the committed column,
# interleaved: the sitting's own build +1.49% mean (worst 3.2%), a same-flags
# rebuild made 2026-09-01 +1.54% (worst 3.2%), homebrew/core's arm64_sequoia
# bottle +13.33% (worst 24.6% on streq, and it goes the OTHER way on loopsum at
# -3.5%, so it is not a uniform offset that could be divided out). The bottle is
# not this column's Rakudo. The rebuild and the original agree with each other
# far more tightly than either agrees with the committed column — arraypush
# 264.3 vs 264.4, rats 238.1 vs 238.1 — so a same-flags rebuild is a sound
# stand-in when the original is gone; these rows use the original anyway,
# because it had not gone.
# RakuAST is slower on 14 of these 16 kernels and faster on two, which is what
# the announcement says to expect while the new backend's optimisation coverage
# catches up (https://dev.to/lizmat/mainstreaming-rakuast-49j8). Read it as a
# 2026.08 snapshot of a backend still landing, not as a verdict on it.
# era      released    kernel      ms      mode
# 2026.09 (released 2026-09-28), measured 2026-09-30 with the method above —
# tools/measure-rakudo-modes.raku, 20 rounds x 4 passes, lanes interleaved,
# minimum — on the homebrew arm64 bottle, same machine (Darwin 27.0.0). 2026.09
# makes RakuAST the default, so here `rakuast` is the plain run and `legacy`
# is RAKUDO_RAKUAST=0; the RAKUDO_LEGACY=1 the announcement named does nothing
# in this build. Each lane was checked to compile with its own grammar
# (Perl6::Grammar / Raku::Grammar) before timing. The two halves of the passes
# agreed within 2% on every cell but mainwhen/rakuast (2.3%). mainwhen is in
# the four-pass set from this era on, and so is multiwhere, timed in its own
# run the same morning: a first run's halves differed by 3.8% while the machine
# settled, a second agreed within 0.6% and gives the rows. The two frontends are within 6% on 14 of
# 17 kernels; RakuAST is faster on streq (0.81x), startup (0.88x) and loopsum
# A SIXTH COLUMN: the MACHINE a row was timed on.
# Rows without it are the Apple M3's, every row above. Rows below carry `m4`:
# an Apple M4 (MacBook Air, Mac16,12, macOS 26.6.2), standing in from
# 2026-10-21 while the M3 is out of reach. gen-dashboard reads one machine's
# rows at a time and gives an M4 bench point only the M4's Rakudo, so a
# Raku++ reading is never compared with a Rakudo timed on the other machine.
# 2026.09 on the M4, measured 2026-10-21 with the method above:
# tools/measure-rakudo-modes.raku, 20 rounds x 4 passes, lanes interleaved,
# minimum, on the homebrew arm64 bottle (arm64_tahoe), the same build the M3's
# 2026.09 rows used. It was installed through /opt/homebrew/bin/brew by full
# path: this box also has an x86_64 Homebrew under /usr/local, first on PATH,
# whose Rakudo would run under Rosetta 2. Both the binary and libmoar are
# arm64-only, and it reports `arm64` at run time. Each lane was checked to
# compile with its own grammar before timing. The halves agreed within 2.7%,
# with 8 of 36 cells over 2%, most of them the second half reading faster as
# the machine settled.
# Against the M3's bottle rows the M4 takes 0.870x (loopsum) to 0.941x
# (arraypush) of the time. As a check, rakubrew's from-source 2026.09 on the
# same M4 was timed the same way at the end of the sitting (halves within
# 1.4%). It reads 0.875x-1.010x of the bottle, about 0.96x at the median, a
# smaller gap than the 13% the 2026.08 note above found on the M3. It is not
# charted: the bottle stays this column's Rakudo on both machines.
# era      released    kernel      ms      mode     machine
